customers(id, name):
1 Ana
2 Ben
3 Cleo
4 Dan

orders(id, customer_id, item):
101, 1, pen
102, 1, book
103, 3, mug

If I run SELECT c.name, o.item FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id, how many rows come back, and what are they?

Three rows:

| name | item |
|---|---|
| Ana | pen |
| Ana | book |
| Cleo | mug |

How to see it without running anything: an inner JOIN keeps only pairs where the ON condition matches. Ana (id 1) matches two orders, so she appears twice. Cleo (id 3) matches one. Ben and Dan have no orders, so they vanish completely — an inner join shows no trace of them. And no order is orphaned here (every customer_id exists in customers), so nothing is lost from the orders side either.

Rule of thumb: the inner join's row count is the number of matching pairs, not the size of either table.

customers(id, name): Ana(1), Ben(2), Cleo(3), Dan(4). orders(id, customer_id, item): (101, 1, pen), (102, 1, book), (103, 3, mug). What changes if I use LEFT JOIN instead of JOIN to pair customers with their order items?

You get five rows instead of three:

| name | item |
|---|---|
| Ana | pen |
| Ana | book |
| Ben | NULL |
| Cleo | mug |
| Dan | NULL |

A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (customers) at least once. Customers with orders behave exactly as in the inner join. Customers without orders — Ben and Dan — still appear, with NULL filling every column that would have come from orders.

That is the whole point of the LEFT variant: the left table is fully preserved, and NULL is the marker for "no match on the right." If you then filter WHERE o.item IS NULL, you have turned it into a finder for customers who never ordered.

Tables: customers(id, name) with Ana(1), Ben(2), Cleo(3), Dan(4); orders(id, customer_id) with two orders for customer 1 and one for customer 3. Write SQL that counts orders per customer, including customers with zero orders, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY c.name;
```

```json
[
  {"name": "Ana", "orders": 2},
  {"name": "Ben", "orders": 0},
  {"name": "Cleo", "orders": 1},
  {"name": "Dan", "orders": 0}
]
```

Two details do the work. The LEFT JOIN keeps Ben and Dan in the result with NULL order columns, and COUNT(o.id) — not COUNT(*) — counts only non-NULL order ids, so they correctly land on 0. COUNT(*) would count their padded rows and report 1 order each.

My employees table has 5 people: 3 in Sales, 2 in Tech. I joined it to a dept_budgets table on dept_id to attach budget info, and the result had 10 rows. Nobody was added to the company — where did the extra 5 rows come from?

From the budgets table having two rows per department — say one row for 2025 and one for 2026. A join matches on the condition you give it, and dept_id alone does not pick a year, so every employee matches both budget rows for their department:

- 3 Sales employees × 2 Sales budget rows = 6 rows
- 2 Tech employees × 2 Tech budget rows = 4 rows
- Total: 10 rows

This is called fan-out: when the join key is not unique on one side, each row on the other side gets duplicated once per match. It is not a bug in the join — the join did exactly what the condition said.

Fixes, depending on what you want: add the year to the ON condition (ON e.dept_id = b.dept_id AND b.year = 2026) to get back to 5 rows, or aggregate budgets to one row per department first if you genuinely want both years combined. The habit to build: before joining, ask "is my key unique on each side?" If it is unique on only one side, predict the multiplication before you run it.

employees(id, name, manager_id):
1, Ruth, NULL
2, Sam, 1
3, Tia, 1
4, Uma, 2

Write SQL listing each employee next to their manager's name, including the person at the top who has no manager. Show the result.

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY e.id;
```

```json
[
  {"employee": "Ruth", "manager": null},
  {"employee": "Sam", "manager": "Ruth"},
  {"employee": "Tia", "manager": "Ruth"},
  {"employee": "Uma", "manager": "Sam"}
]
```

This is a self join: the same table appears twice under two aliases, e for the employee and m for the manager row being looked up. The LEFT JOIN matters — Ruth's manager_id is NULL, so an inner join would silently drop the boss from her own org chart.
customers(id, name): Ana(1), Ben(2), Cleo(3), Dan(4). orders(id, customer_id): (101, 1), (102, 1), (103, 3). How do I find the customers who have never placed an order?

Use a LEFT JOIN and keep only the rows where the right side failed to match:

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

Result: Ben and Dan.

Why it works: the LEFT JOIN preserves every customer, padding the order columns with NULL when there is no matching order. Filtering on o.id IS NULL keeps exactly those padded rows. Pick a right-side column that can never be NULL in real data — the primary key is the safe choice, since a matched row always has one.

This pattern is called an anti-join: "rows in A with no partner in B." You will also see it written with NOT EXISTS, which does the same job and is safer than NOT IN when NULLs might be lurking in the subquery.

price_tiers(tier, min_price, max_price):
low, 0, 9.99
mid, 10, 49.99
high, 50, 9999

products(name, price): cable 5, mouse 25, keyboard 25, monitor 80.

Can a join assign each product its tier even though there is no tier column anywhere to match on?

Yes — a join condition does not have to be an equality. This is a range join (also called a band join):

```sql
SELECT p.name, p.price, t.tier
FROM products p
JOIN price_tiers t ON p.price BETWEEN t.min_price AND t.max_price;
```

Result, 4 rows:

| name | price | tier |
|---|---|---|
| cable | 5 | low |
| mouse | 25 | mid |
| keyboard | 25 | mid |
| monitor | 80 | high |

Each product falls inside exactly one band, so each appears exactly once. The thing to watch: if the bands overlapped — say mid ran to 59.99 — the monitor at 80 would still be fine, but a 55 product would match two tiers and appear twice. With range joins, the row count is "one row per band the value falls into," so clean, non-overlapping bands are what keep the result honest.

students(id, name): Ivy(1), Jay(2). courses(id, title): Art(10), Bio(20). enrollments(student_id, course_id): (1, 10), (1, 20), (2, 20). Write SQL that lists student names next to the course titles they are enrolled in, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
ORDER BY s.name, c.title;
```

```json
[
  {"name": "Ivy", "title": "Art"},
  {"name": "Ivy", "title": "Bio"},
  {"name": "Jay", "title": "Bio"}
]
```

Students and courses have a many-to-many relationship, which is why the enrollments table sits between them: neither side can hold the other's key without repeating. The query walks the bridge — student to their enrollment rows, enrollment rows to course titles — and each enrollment row produces exactly one output row, so 3 enrollments give 3 pairs.
I have a colors table with 3 rows (red, green, blue) and a sizes table with 4 rows (S, M, L, XL). Someone told me a CROSS JOIN of these gives 12 rows. Why 12, and when would I actually want that?

A CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of the other — the full cartesian product. 3 colors × 4 sizes = 12 combinations: red-S, red-M, red-L, red-XL, green-S, and so on through blue-XL.

That is exactly what you want when the goal is all combinations: generating a variant matrix for a product catalog, building a schedule grid of every room against every time slot, or producing every date × store pair so a report can show zeros where nothing sold.

The danger is doing it by accident. The classic accident is joining two tables and forgetting the ON condition in an engine or syntax that treats it as a cross join: a 10,000-row table crossed with a 10,000-row table is 100 million rows. So the rule is: CROSS JOIN on purpose, in writing, with small inputs — and if a join result ever comes back with row count equal to left rows × right rows, suspect a missing condition first.

customers: Ana(1), Ben(2), Cleo(3), Dan(4). orders(customer_id, item): (1, pen), (1, book), (3, mug). I wrote a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders and added WHERE o.item = 'mug' to find mug buyers, but Ben and Dan disappeared from the output even though I used LEFT. I wanted every customer listed, with the mug shown only where it exists. What went wrong?

The WHERE clause undid the LEFT JOIN. Walk it through: the join first produces five rows, with Ben and Dan padded by NULL items. Then WHERE o.item = 'mug' tests every row — and for Ben and Dan, NULL = 'mug' is not true (it is UNKNOWN), so their rows are filtered out. Ana's pen and book rows also fail the test. Only Cleo's mug row survives: 1 row, and the LEFT JOIN might as well have been an inner join.

The fix is to move the condition into the ON clause, where it controls matching instead of filtering finished rows:

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.item
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.item = 'mug';
```

Now the join only matches mug orders; customers without one still appear with NULL:

| name | item |
|---|---|
| Ana | NULL |
| Ben | NULL |
| Cleo | mug |
| Dan | NULL |

Memory rule: conditions on the right table of a LEFT JOIN belong in ON if you want to preserve left rows; conditions in WHERE run after the join and treat NULL-padded rows as failures.
authors(id, name): Octavia(1), Ursula(2). books(id, author_id, pages): (1, 1, 320), (2, 1, 288), (3, 2, 416). Write SQL giving total pages written per author, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT a.name, SUM(b.pages) AS total_pages
FROM authors a
JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.name
ORDER BY total_pages DESC;
```

```json
[
  {"name": "Octavia", "total_pages": 608},
  {"name": "Ursula", "total_pages": 416}
]
```

The join fans each author out to one row per book (Octavia twice, Ursula once), and GROUP BY collapses those rows back down, summing pages within each pile: 320 + 288 = 608 for Octavia. Join-then-group is the standard rhythm — the join assembles the detail rows, the aggregation reduces them.

shelf_a(item) has: fig, kiwi. shelf_b(item) has: kiwi, plum. I want one list showing every item and which shelves hold it, including items that are on only one shelf. INNER and LEFT joins each seem to miss something. What is the right tool?

A FULL OUTER JOIN — it keeps unmatched rows from both sides:

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(a.item, b.item) AS item,
       a.item IS NOT NULL AS on_a,
       b.item IS NOT NULL AS on_b
FROM shelf_a a
FULL JOIN shelf_b b ON b.item = a.item;
```

Result, 3 rows:

| item | on_a | on_b |
|---|---|---|
| fig | true | false |
| kiwi | true | true |
| plum | false | true |

Why the others fall short: an INNER JOIN returns only kiwi, the overlap. A LEFT JOIN from shelf_a keeps fig and kiwi but never mentions plum. FULL JOIN is the union of both preservations: matched pairs merge into one row, and anything unmatched appears with NULLs on the missing side. COALESCE picks whichever side's item is present for display.

One portability note: a few engines (notably SQLite and older MySQL) have no FULL JOIN keyword. There, emulate it with a LEFT JOIN UNION an anti-join of the right side — same three rows, more typing.
t1(k, v): (7, a), (7, b), (8, c). t2(k, w): (7, x), (7, y), (7, z), (9, w). Both tables are tiny, but SELECT * FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON t1.k = t2.k returned 6 rows. Trace exactly where 6 comes from.

The join multiplies match counts per key value. For each key, output rows = (rows with that key in t1) × (rows with that key in t2):

- k = 7: t1 has 2 rows (a, b), t2 has 3 rows (x, y, z) → 2 × 3 = 6 rows: (a,x), (a,y), (a,z), (b,x), (b,y), (b,z)
- k = 8: t2 has no 8 → 0 rows; t1's (8, c) disappears
- k = 9: t1 has no 9 → 0 rows; t2's (9, w) disappears

Total: 6 rows, all with k = 7.

The general rule: a join is safe from surprises when the key is unique on at least one side. When the key is duplicated on both sides, the counts multiply — this is the most explosive form of fan-out, and on real tables it is how a join of two modest tables produces a billion rows. Defenses: deduplicate one side first (SELECT DISTINCT, or aggregate it to one row per key), or confirm with a quick GROUP BY k HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on each side before joining, so you know the multiplication factor in advance.
products(id, name): soap(1), rope(2), tape(3). sales(product_id): 1, 1, 3. Write SQL listing products that have never been sold, using NOT EXISTS, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM sales s
  WHERE s.product_id = p.id
);
```

```json
[
  {"id": 2, "name": "rope"}
]
```

Product 1 appears in sales (twice — duplicates do not matter, existence is binary), product 3 appears once, and product 2 never appears, so rope is the only row. NOT EXISTS is the NULL-safe way to write an anti-join: it asks "does any matching row exist?" and a NULL product_id in sales simply never matches anything, instead of poisoning the whole result the way NOT IN can.

regions(id, region_name): (1, North), (2, South). customers(id, name, region_id): Ana(1, region 1), Ben(2, region 1), Cleo(3, region 2), Dan(4, region 2). orders(customer_id, item): (1, pen), (1, book), (3, mug). Walk me through what SELECT c.name, o.item, r.region_name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN regions r ON r.id = c.region_id returns.

Three rows:

| name | item | region_name |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | pen | North |
| Ana | book | North |
| Cleo | mug | South |

Walk it in stages. Start from orders, since that is the FROM table: 3 order rows. The first join attaches each order's customer — every order has a valid customer_id, so still 3 rows, now carrying Ana, Ana, Cleo. The second join attaches each customer's region: Ana is region 1 (North), Cleo is region 2 (South). Still 3 rows.

Notice who never appears: Ben and Dan. Chained inner joins filter at every step — a row must survive every join to reach the output, and since Ben and Dan have no orders, they were never in the pipeline. Each join in a chain is an independent gate: it can only keep or multiply the rows it receives, based on its own condition.
teammates(id, name, team): Al(1, red), Bo(2, red), Cy(3, red), Di(4, blue). Write SQL listing every pair of distinct people who share a team, each pair exactly once, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT a.name AS person1, b.name AS person2
FROM teammates a
JOIN teammates b ON a.team = b.team AND a.id < b.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;
```

```json
[
  {"person1": "Al", "person2": "Bo"},
  {"person1": "Al", "person2": "Cy"},
  {"person1": "Bo", "person2": "Cy"}
]
```

Red has three members, giving 3 choose 2 = 3 pairs; blue has only Di, so no pairs. The a.id < b.id condition does two jobs: it excludes self-pairs (Al with Al) and it keeps only one ordering of each pair (Al–Bo, not also Bo–Al). Drop that condition and the same-team self join returns 9 red rows — every member paired with every member including themselves, in both directions — which is the raw material this condition trims down to the 3 real pairs.

sales(rep, amount):
Kim, 10
Lee, 20
Kim, 5
Lee, 7
Kim, 3

Explain what SELECT rep, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY rep actually does, step by step, like I have never seen GROUP BY before.

Picture GROUP BY as sorting the rows into piles, one pile per distinct rep value:

- Kim pile: 10, 5, 3
- Lee pile: 20, 7

Then SUM(amount) is computed once per pile, and each pile collapses into a single output row:

| rep | sum |
|---|---|
| Kim | 18 |
| Lee | 27 |

Three ideas to keep. First, the output has one row per group — 5 rows in, 2 rows out. Second, any column you SELECT must either be the grouping column or wrapped in an aggregate (SUM, COUNT, AVG...), because after the collapse there is no single "amount" for the Kim pile, only the pile's total. Third, grouping happens before any ORDER BY: if you add ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC, Lee's 27 sorts above Kim's 18.
visits(day, visitor): (Mon, u1), (Mon, u2), (Mon, u1), (Tue, u1). For each day, I want both the number of visit rows and the number of distinct visitors. Write the SQL and show the result.

```sql
SELECT day,
       COUNT(*) AS visit_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT visitor) AS distinct_visitors
FROM visits
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day;
```

```json
[
  {"day": "Mon", "visit_rows": 3, "distinct_visitors": 2},
  {"day": "Tue", "visit_rows": 1, "distinct_visitors": 1}
]
```

Monday has 3 rows but only 2 distinct visitors, because u1 visited twice. COUNT(*) counts rows in the pile; COUNT(DISTINCT visitor) first throws away duplicate values within the pile, then counts. "How much traffic" and "how many people" are different questions — this is how you ask both at once.

orders(customer, amount): Ana 30, Ana 80, Ben 10, Cleo 60, Cleo 60. I want customers whose total spending is over 100. I tried putting SUM(amount) > 100 in the WHERE clause and it failed. Why, and what is the correct form? Also: what changes if I add WHERE amount > 50 to the correct query?

WHERE runs before grouping, when the table is still individual rows and SUM(amount) does not exist yet — there is no total to test. Filters on aggregates belong in HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY has built the totals:

```sql
SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(amount) > 100;
```

Totals: Ana 30 + 80 = 110, Ben 10, Cleo 60 + 60 = 120. Result: Ana (110) and Cleo (120).

Now add WHERE amount > 50 and the story changes, because WHERE trims rows before they ever reach a pile. Ana keeps only her 80 (the 30 is discarded), so her total becomes 80 and she fails HAVING. Ben's only row is discarded, so Ben has no pile at all. Cleo keeps both 60s and still totals 120. Result with the WHERE: Cleo only.

The mental model is a pipeline: WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY piles them, HAVING filters piles, ORDER BY sorts what is left.
survey(id, answer): (1, yes), (2, NULL), (3, no), (4, yes). I ran three counts and got 4, 3, and 2. Which count gives which number, and why?

- COUNT(*) = 4 — it counts rows, all of them, whatever they contain.
- COUNT(answer) = 3 — it counts rows where answer is not NULL, so respondent 2, who skipped the question, is excluded.
- COUNT(CASE WHEN answer = 'yes' THEN 1 END) = 2 — or equivalently SUM(answer = 'yes') in some engines; it counts only the yes rows: 1 and 4.

The general principle: COUNT(*) is about the table, COUNT(column) is about the values. The gap between them is exactly your NULL count, which makes COUNT(*) − COUNT(answer) a quick data-quality check for "how many blanks do I have?" Run the pair on any column you care about and the difference tells you how much missing data you are carrying.

temps(day, reading): (Mon, 20), (Tue, NULL), (Wed, 22), (Thu, 24). A sensor missed Tuesday. Write SQL for the average reading and show the result — and be careful, I almost computed it by hand as 16.5.

tickets(channel, priority):
web, high
web, low
web, high
phone, high
phone, low
phone, low

How do I get a count for every channel–priority combination, and what are the counts?

Group by both columns:

```sql
SELECT channel, priority, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM tickets
GROUP BY channel, priority;
```

| channel | priority | n |
|---|---|---|
| web | high | 2 |
| web | low | 1 |
| phone | high | 1 |
| phone | low | 2 |

GROUP BY with two keys makes piles within piles: first split by channel (3 web rows, 3 phone rows), then split each of those by priority. Six rows in, four combinations out — one output row per distinct combination that actually occurs. Combinations with no rows (say, an email channel nobody used) do not appear at all; GROUP BY only reports piles that exist.

The order of the keys does not change the counts — GROUP BY priority, channel gives the same four numbers, just presented differently. Key order matters only for how the output reads and how a matching ORDER BY lines up.

orders(month, status):
Jan, paid
Jan, paid
Jan, refunded
Feb, paid
Feb, refunded
Feb, refunded

I want one row per month with separate counts of paid and refunded orders side by side. Write the SQL and show the result.

```sql
SELECT month,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS refunded
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
```

```json
[
  {"month": "Jan", "paid": 2, "refunded": 1},
  {"month": "Feb", "paid": 1, "refunded": 2}
]
```

This is conditional aggregation: inside each month's pile, the CASE turns every row into a 1 or a 0 for a given status, and SUM adds the 1s. It pivots a status column into side-by-side columns without a second pass over the table. The ELSE 0 matters — without it, non-matching rows produce NULL, and while SUM would skip those anyway, being explicit keeps COUNT-style variants of the same trick from surprising you.
readings(room, temp): kitchen 21, kitchen 23, kitchen 19, hall 18, hall 18. Write SQL showing the minimum and maximum temperature per room, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT room, MIN(temp) AS min_temp, MAX(temp) AS max_temp
FROM readings
GROUP BY room
ORDER BY room;
```

```json
[
  {"room": "hall", "min_temp": 18, "max_temp": 18},
  {"room": "kitchen", "min_temp": 19, "max_temp": 23}
]
```

MIN and MAX are per-pile like any aggregate: the kitchen pile (21, 23, 19) yields 19 and 23, and the hall pile (18, 18) yields 18 twice. When min equals max, as in the hall, the pile held a single distinct value — a useful quick check for sensors that are stuck reporting one number.

sales(rep, product, amount): (Kim, pen, 10), (Kim, book, 5), (Lee, mug, 7). I wrote SELECT rep, product, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY rep, expecting one row per rep. Postgres rejected it. A colleague says their MySQL just ran it and showed a product. Who is right, and what is the real problem with my query?

Postgres is right, and your colleague's MySQL result is quietly meaningless. Think about what the query asks for: GROUP BY rep collapses Kim's two rows into one pile. SUM(amount) is well-defined for the pile: 15. But product? Kim's pile contains two products, pen and book, and the output has room for only one value. There is no correct answer — the question itself is malformed.

That is the rule standard SQL enforces: in a grouped query, every selected column must be either a grouping key or wrapped in an aggregate. Postgres and MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY enabled reject anything else. Older or loosely configured MySQL instead picks an arbitrary row from the pile and shows its product — pen or book depending on internal order you cannot see or control. The query "works" and lies.

Your options, depending on intent: group by both (GROUP BY rep, product gives 3 rows), aggregate the product too if a summary makes sense (for example STRING_AGG or GROUP_CONCAT to list both), or drop product from the SELECT. What you cannot do is have one row per rep and a single product, because the data does not contain that fact.
purchases(customer, amount): (Mia, 25), (Mia, 40), (Noah, 90), (Mia, 10), (Noah, 5), (Zoe, 60). Write SQL ranking customers by total spend, highest first, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM purchases
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY total DESC;
```

```json
[
  {"customer": "Noah", "total": 95},
  {"customer": "Mia", "total": 75},
  {"customer": "Zoe", "total": 60}
]
```

Totals first: Noah 90 + 5 = 95, Mia 25 + 40 + 10 = 75, Zoe 60. Note that ORDER BY references the alias total — aliases defined in the SELECT list are legal in ORDER BY (and in HAVING on most engines), even though they are not legal in WHERE, because ORDER BY runs after the select list has been computed.

orders(id, total): (1, 100), (2, 60). shipments(order_id): order 1 has 3 shipments, order 2 has 1. I joined orders to shipments so I could count shipments per order, and while I was there I also summed order totals — got 360. Total order value should be 160. Explain the discrepancy.

Your SUM was computed after the join, and the join had already multiplied the orders. Joining on order_id produces 4 rows: order 1 appears 3 times (once per shipment), order 2 appears once. SUM(total) over those rows is 100 + 100 + 100 + 60 = 360. The total was never wrong in the table — it was counted three times because the join repeated the row carrying it.

This is the fan-out trap applied to aggregates, and it is more dangerous than fan-out in a plain listing because the result looks like a plausible number, not an obvious duplication.

Two clean fixes:

1. Aggregate each side separately, then join the summaries:

```sql
SELECT o.id, o.total, s.shipments
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS shipments
      FROM shipments GROUP BY order_id) s ON s.order_id = o.id;
```

2. Or, if you only need the grand total, sum from orders alone — never sum a column from the "one" side of a one-to-many join after joining.

Rule of thumb: the moment a query both joins one-to-many and aggregates, check which table each aggregated column belongs to. Columns from the many side aggregate fine; columns from the one side get silently repeated.

readings(room, value): room A has two rows, both NULL (sensor offline all day); room B has one row, value 5. SELECT room, SUM(value) FROM readings GROUP BY room gave me NULL for room A instead of 0. Is that a bug?

Not a bug — it is the defined behavior, and arguably the honest one. SUM over a pile of nothing-but-NULL has no numbers to add, so SQL returns NULL: "no data" rather than "zero." Room B's pile has a real 5, so it reports 5.

| room | sum |
|---|---|
| A | NULL |
| B | 5 |

The distinction matters downstream: NULL propagates (NULL + anything is NULL), so a grand total built from these group sums would vanish if you added them naively. If your report wants offline to read as 0, say so explicitly:

```sql
SELECT room, COALESCE(SUM(value), 0) AS total
FROM readings
GROUP BY room;
```

COALESCE replaces the NULL result with 0 after aggregation. Choose deliberately: keep NULL when "we don't know" is the truth worth preserving, coalesce when the consumer of the report genuinely needs a number.
votes(option) has 7 rows: A, A, B, A, C, B, A. Write SQL showing each option's vote count and its percentage of all votes, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT option,
       COUNT(*) AS votes,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM votes
GROUP BY option
ORDER BY votes DESC;
```

```json
[
  {"option": "A", "votes": 4, "pct": 57.1},
  {"option": "B", "votes": 2, "pct": 28.6},
  {"option": "C", "votes": 1, "pct": 14.3}
]
```

Counts: A 4, B 2, C 1, total 7. The trick is SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () — a window function applied to the grouped counts, giving the grand total (7) on every row so each group can divide by it. Percentages: 4/7 = 57.1%, 2/7 = 28.6%, 1/7 = 14.3%. The 100.0 (not 100) forces decimal division; with integers, 100 * 4 / 7 in some engines truncates to 57 before you ever see a decimal.

payments(customer, method): (Ana, card), (Ana, card), (Ana, cash), (Ben, card). How many distinct payment methods has each customer used? And how is that different from running SELECT DISTINCT customer, method?

Distinct methods per customer: Ana 2 (card, cash), Ben 1 (card).

```sql
SELECT customer, COUNT(DISTINCT method) AS methods
FROM payments
GROUP BY customer;
```

COUNT(DISTINCT method) deduplicates inside each customer's pile before counting: Ana's pile holds card, card, cash, which collapses to {card, cash} and counts 2. Her duplicate card payment inflates a plain COUNT(method) to 3 but is invisible here.

SELECT DISTINCT customer, method answers a different question — it lists the combinations that exist, returning 3 rows: (Ana, card), (Ana, cash), (Ben, card). That is a roster, not a count. The confusion between them is common: DISTINCT in the SELECT list dedupes output rows; DISTINCT inside an aggregate dedupes values within each group before the aggregate sees them. Same keyword, different stage of the pipeline.
sales(day, amount): (Mon, 10), (Tue, 20), (Wed, 15). I want a running total column: 10, 30, 45. I know GROUP BY will not do this. What will?

A window function — SUM with an OVER clause:

```sql
SELECT day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running_total
FROM sales;
```

| day | amount | running_total |
|---|---|---|
| Mon | 10 | 10 |
| Tue | 20 | 30 |
| Wed | 15 | 45 |

How to read the OVER clause: "for each row, sum amount over all rows from the start up to and including this one, in day order." Unlike GROUP BY, nothing collapses — you get one output row per input row, with the aggregate computed over a sliding window that ends at the current row.

That is the defining trait of window functions: the aggregate is attached to each row instead of replacing the rows. One caution: the running total follows the ORDER BY inside OVER, so the days must sort the way you mean — use real dates or a sequence number, not weekday names, once you leave this toy example ('Fri' sorts before 'Mon' alphabetically).
scores(student, subject, score): (Ivy, math, 90), (Jay, math, 85), (Ivy, art, 70), (Jay, art, 88). Write SQL numbering the students within each subject by score, best first, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT student, subject, score,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY subject ORDER BY score DESC) AS rn
FROM scores
ORDER BY subject, rn;
```

```json
[
  {"student": "Jay", "subject": "art", "score": 88, "rn": 1},
  {"student": "Ivy", "subject": "art", "score": 70, "rn": 2},
  {"student": "Ivy", "subject": "math", "score": 90, "rn": 1},
  {"student": "Jay", "subject": "math", "score": 85, "rn": 2}
]
```

PARTITION BY subject restarts the numbering for each subject — it is the window-function cousin of GROUP BY, except rows survive instead of collapsing. In math, Ivy's 90 takes rn 1; in art, Jay's 88 does. The outer ORDER BY only arranges the display; the numbering was decided entirely inside the OVER clause.
Leaderboard: Ana 100, Ben 90, Cleo 90, Dan 80. RANK, DENSE_RANK, and ROW_NUMBER all claim to rank this. Give me the exact output of each and tell me which one a podium should use.

All three order by points descending; they differ only in how they treat the tie at 90:

| name | points | RANK | DENSE_RANK | ROW_NUMBER |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ana | 100 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Ben | 90 | 2 | 2 | 2 |
| Cleo | 90 | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| Dan | 80 | 4 | 3 | 4 |

RANK gives tied rows the same rank, then skips: two people hold rank 2, so the next rank is 4 — it answers "how many rows are strictly ahead of me?" DENSE_RANK also shares ranks but never skips, so Dan is 3rd: it answers "how many distinct scores are ahead of me?" ROW_NUMBER ignores the tie entirely and hands out 2 and 3 in an unspecified order — Ben might get 3 tomorrow if the engine's internal order changes.

For a podium, use RANK or DENSE_RANK: Ben and Cleo genuinely tied, and any ranking that separates them is inventing a difference. Choose RANK if rank should mean "position in line" (there is no 3rd place when two share 2nd and someone follows), DENSE_RANK if every distinct score should get the next integer. Never use ROW_NUMBER where ties are real — it manufactures a winner out of storage order.
monthly(month, revenue): (2026-01, 1000), (2026-02, 1200), (2026-03, 900). Write SQL showing each month's revenue, the previous month's revenue, and the change. Show the result.

```sql
SELECT month, revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly;
```

```json
[
  {"month": "2026-01", "revenue": 1000, "prev_revenue": null, "change": null},
  {"month": "2026-02", "revenue": 1200, "prev_revenue": 1000, "change": 200},
  {"month": "2026-03", "revenue": 900, "prev_revenue": 1200, "change": -300}
]
```

LAG reaches one row back in the window's ordering and pulls a value down into the current row. The first month has no predecessor, so prev_revenue is NULL — and the change is NULL too, because arithmetic on NULL yields NULL. That is the honest answer for a first period: not zero change, unknown change. One ordering warning: the months here are ISO strings (2026-01, 2026-02), which sort chronologically. Had they been names like Jan, Feb, Mar, ORDER BY month would sort them alphabetically — Feb, Jan, Mar — and LAG would happily compute changes against the wrong predecessor. Order windows by real dates or sortable keys, never by display labels.

employees(dept, name, salary): (Sales, Kim, 50), (Sales, Lee, 70), (Tech, Mel, 90), (Tech, Ned, 60). I want every employee listed with their department's average salary next to them. GROUP BY dept gives me only 2 rows. How do I keep all 4?

Use AVG as a window function with PARTITION BY:

```sql
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
FROM employees;
```

| dept | name | salary | dept_avg |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sales | Kim | 50 | 60 |
| Sales | Lee | 70 | 60 |
| Tech | Mel | 90 | 75 |
| Tech | Ned | 60 | 75 |

Sales average: (50 + 70) / 2 = 60. Tech: (90 + 60) / 2 = 75. PARTITION BY dept tells the window function to compute the average separately within each department, and the result is stamped onto every row of that department instead of collapsing the rows into one.

The contrast to remember: GROUP BY dept with AVG answers "what is each department's average?" in 2 rows. AVG OVER (PARTITION BY dept) answers "what is each employee's department average?" in 4 rows. Same aggregate, different question — the OVER clause is what keeps the detail rows alive.
movements(item, day, delta): (A, 1, +5), (A, 2, -2), (B, 1, +7), (A, 3, +4), (B, 2, -1). Write SQL showing the running stock level of each item after each movement, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT item, day, delta,
       SUM(delta) OVER (PARTITION BY item ORDER BY day) AS stock
FROM movements
ORDER BY item, day;
```

```json
[
  {"item": "A", "day": 1, "delta": 5, "stock": 5},
  {"item": "A", "day": 2, "delta": -2, "stock": 3},
  {"item": "A", "day": 3, "delta": 4, "stock": 7},
  {"item": "B", "day": 1, "delta": 7, "stock": 7},
  {"item": "B", "day": 2, "delta": -1, "stock": 6}
]
```

Two partitions run independently: item A accumulates 5, then 5 − 2 = 3, then 3 + 4 = 7; item B accumulates 7, then 7 − 1 = 6. Without PARTITION BY item, the sum would run across both items mixed together in day order and produce meaningless stock levels. The partition is what makes this "running total per thing" instead of "running total of everything.

Daily temperatures for days 1-4: 10, 20, 30, 40. I want a 3-day moving average. Someone wrote AVG(temp) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Compute what that gives for each day, and explain why day 1 is not an error or a NULL.

| day | temp | moving_avg |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | 10 |
| 2 | 20 | 15 |
| 3 | 30 | 20 |
| 4 | 40 | 30 |

The frame ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means "the current row and up to two physical rows before it." At the start of the table the frame just gets clipped — there are no rows before day 1, so its frame is {10} alone and the average is 10. Day 2's frame is {10, 20} → 15. Only from day 3 on does the frame hold a full 3 rows: {10, 20, 30} → 20, then it slides: {20, 30, 40} → 30. A short frame at the boundary is normal behavior, not missing data; if you need full windows only, filter afterwards on ROW_NUMBER or a count of frame rows.

One distinction worth burning in: this query says ROWS, counting physical rows. The default frame when you write only ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which groups peer rows — rows whose ORDER BY values are equal get the same aggregate, computed including all peers. With duplicate days, ROWS and RANGE give different answers, and picking the wrong one is a classic silent discrepancy.

products(category, name, price): fruit — apple 3, pear 5, plum 4; veg — carrot 2, kale 6. How do I get the top 2 most expensive products in each category? A plain ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 2 only gives me kale and pear overall.

Rank inside each category first, then filter on the rank:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, name, price,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC) AS rn
  FROM products
)
SELECT category, name, price
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY category, price DESC;
```

Result:

| category | name | price |
|---|---|---|
| fruit | pear | 5 |
| fruit | plum | 4 |
| veg | kale | 6 |
| veg | carrot | 2 |

Why the two-step shape: window functions are computed after WHERE, so you cannot filter on rn in the same query level — the rank does not exist yet when WHERE runs. Wrapping the ranked rows in a CTE (or subquery) makes rn a real column that an outer WHERE can test. PARTITION BY category restarts the ranking per category, which is the part your global LIMIT could not express. If ties at the cutoff should both be included, swap ROW_NUMBER for RANK and accept that a category may return 3 rows.

spending(dept, person, spent): (Sales, Ana, 30), (Sales, Ben, 70), (Tech, Cleo, 90), (Tech, Dan, 10). Write SQL showing each person's spending and what percentage of their department's total it is. Show the result.

```sql
SELECT dept, person, spent,
       ROUND(100.0 * spent / SUM(spent) OVER (PARTITION BY dept), 1) AS pct_of_dept
FROM spending
ORDER BY dept, spent DESC;
```

```json
[
  {"dept": "Sales", "person": "Ben", "spent": 70, "pct_of_dept": 70.0},
  {"dept": "Sales", "person": "Ana", "spent": 30, "pct_of_dept": 30.0},
  {"dept": "Tech", "person": "Cleo", "spent": 90, "pct_of_dept": 90.0},
  {"dept": "Tech", "person": "Dan", "spent": 10, "pct_of_dept": 10.0}
]
```

Both department totals are 100, which makes the arithmetic easy to verify: Sales splits 70/30, Tech splits 90/10. The pattern generalizes to any total: SUM(spent) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) stamps the group total onto each row, and the row divides its own value by it. Multiply by 100.0 — a decimal literal — so the division is decimal rather than integer in engines that distinguish.
logins(day) for one user has three rows: day 1, day 4, day 9 (integers, days since some epoch). I want to know the gap until the user's next login, for each login. How, and what are the gaps?

LAG looks backward; LEAD looks forward:

```sql
SELECT day,
       LEAD(day) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS next_day,
       LEAD(day) OVER (ORDER BY day) - day AS gap
FROM logins;
```

| day | next_day | gap |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 3 |
| 4 | 9 | 5 |
| 9 | NULL | NULL |

The day-1 login is followed 3 days later; the day-4 login, 5 days later. The last login has no successor, so LEAD returns NULL and the subtraction inherits the NULL — which is the correct report: the gap is not zero, it is not yet known.

In real tables the day column would be a timestamp and the gap would come from your engine's date-difference function (DATEDIFF, or subtracting dates, or julianday in SQLite), but the shape is identical: LEAD to fetch the next event into the current row, then subtract. This pattern — fetch the neighbor, compute in place — is how most event-sequence questions (session lengths, time between orders, days since previous purchase) are answered.
signups(day, new_users): (Mon, 3), (Tue, 5), (Wed, 2). Write SQL with a cumulative total of users signed up through each day, and show the result.

```sql
FROM signups;
```

```json
[
  {"day": "Mon", "new_users": 3, "cumulative": 3},
  {"day": "Tue", "new_users": 5, "cumulative": 8},
  {"day": "Wed", "new_users": 2, "cumulative": 10}
]
```

Cumulative: 3, then 3 + 5 = 8, then 8 + 2 = 10. The window's default frame — from the first row through the current row — is exactly a running total. Exam scores: 100, 95, 95, 90, 85. I want "the top 2 scores" but the two 95s are tied and it feels wrong to include one and not the other. Compare filtering on RANK versus ROW_NUMBER with a cutoff of 2.

Rank the five scores first:

| score | RANK | ROW_NUMBER |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 1 | 1 |
| 95 | 2 | 2 |
| 95 | 2 | 3 |
| 90 | 4 | 4 |
| 85 | 5 | 5 |

Filter RANK <= 2 and you get 3 rows: 100, 95, 95. The tie is honored — both 95s hold rank 2, so both pass a "top 2 ranks" cutoff. Filter ROW_NUMBER <= 2 and you get exactly 2 rows: 100 and one of the 95s, chosen by whatever order the engine happened to produce them in. Run it on a different day, plan, or engine version and the other 95 may win.

So the real question is what "top 2" means in your domain. If it means two rows (a report with exactly two lines, a LIMIT-style quota), ROW_NUMBER is honest — but document that ties break arbitrarily, or add a deterministic tiebreaker like ORDER BY score DESC, student_id. If it means two performance levels (everyone at the top two levels gets the prize, the bonus, the interview), RANK is the truthful choice and the row count is allowed to float to 3. Most "top N" bugs are this ambiguity left unstated.

shifts(waiter, tips): (Ana, 10), (Ana, 20), (Ben, 15). I computed average tips two ways. AVG(tips) with GROUP BY waiter gave me 2 rows. AVG(tips) OVER (PARTITION BY waiter) gave me 3 rows — and every value was 15 anyway. Explain both outputs.

Both are correct; they answer different questions.

GROUP BY waiter collapses each waiter's rows into one summary row:

| waiter | avg_tips |
|---|---|
| Ana | 15 |
| Ben | 15 |

Ana's average is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15; Ben has a single shift, so his average is his 15.

The window version computes the same averages but stamps each one back onto every original row:

| waiter | tips | avg_tips |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | 10 | 15 |
| Ana | 20 | 15 |
| Ben | 15 | 15 |

Three rows in, three rows out — window functions never reduce the row count; they annotate. The averages coincide at 15 here, which makes the outputs look redundant, but the shapes differ in the way that matters: only the window version can feed a follow-up comparison per row, like "which of Ana's shifts beat her own average?" (her 20-tip shift). Rule of thumb: GROUP BY when the group is the unit of the answer; a window function when the row is the unit and the group is just context.
prices(item, day, price): (milk, 1, 3), (milk, 2, 4), (milk, 3, 4), (eggs, 1, 2), (eggs, 2, 5). Write SQL returning one row per item with its most recent price, and show the result.

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT item, price,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY item ORDER BY day DESC) AS rn
  FROM prices
)
SELECT item, price AS latest_price
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY item;
```

```json
[
  {"item": "eggs", "latest_price": 5},
  {"item": "milk", "latest_price": 4}
]
```

Within each item's partition, ordering by day descending puts the newest row first, so rn = 1 is the latest price: milk's day-3 price of 4 (not its day-1 price of 3), eggs' day-2 price of 5. This "rank descending, keep rn = 1" pattern is the standard way to fetch the latest record per group. One caveat: if two rows for an item share the maximum day, ROW_NUMBER picks one arbitrarily — add a tiebreaker (an id or timestamp) if your data can contain same-day duplicates.

Eight runners finished with times (seconds): 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17. I want to split them into 4 performance quartiles labeled 1 to 4, fastest quartile = 1. What does NTILE do with this, exactly?

NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY time) deals the ordered rows into 4 buckets as evenly as it can:

| time | quartile |
|---|---|
| 10 | 1 |
| 11 | 1 |
| 12 | 2 |
| 13 | 2 |
| 14 | 3 |
| 15 | 3 |
| 16 | 4 |
| 17 | 4 |

Eight rows over 4 buckets is a clean 2 per bucket. When the count does not divide evenly, the earlier buckets absorb the extras: 9 rows in NTILE(4) gives bucket sizes 3, 2, 2, 2 — never 2, 2, 2, 3. So bucket 1 is always at least as large as bucket 4.

Two things NTILE does not do: it knows nothing about the values themselves, only their order — if the times were 10, 11, 12, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, the quartiles would still split 2/2/2/2, because NTILE counts rows, not ranges. And tied times at a boundary can be split across buckets arbitrarily, since the ordering among equals is unspecified. Use NTILE for "top quarter of finishers," not for "everyone under a threshold.

```sql

  SELECT email, name, updated,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY updated DESC) AS rn
  FROM contacts
)
SELECT email, name, updated
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY email;
```

```json
[
  {"email": "a@x", "name": "Ana R.", "updated": "2026-03-01"},
  {"email": "b@x", "name": "Ben", "updated": "2026-02-01"}
]
```

products(name, price): pen 5, book 12, mug 9, desk 40. Write a query for products priced above the average price, and tell me which products qualify before I run it.

```sql
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
```

Only the desk qualifies. The subquery in parentheses is a scalar subquery: it returns exactly one value, the average (5 + 12 + 9 + 40) / 4 = 66 / 4 = 16.5. The outer query then behaves as if you had written WHERE price > 16.5, and only the desk at 40 clears it — the book at 12 and mug at 9 are below average, however respectable they look next to the pen.

Two properties worth noting. The subquery here is uncorrelated: it does not reference the outer table, so it is conceptually computed once and reused for every row. And the contract is strict — a scalar subquery must return one row and one column. If it could return several values, the comparison price > (list) has no meaning, and the engine will raise an error rather than guess.
customers(id, name): Ana(1), Ben(2), Cleo(3). orders(customer_id) has rows: 1, 1, 3. Write SQL listing customers who have placed at least one order, using IN with a subquery, and show the result.

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
```

```json
[
  {"id": 1, "name": "Ana"},
  {"id": 3, "name": "Cleo"}
]
```

IN is a membership test: a customer passes if their id appears anywhere in the subquery's list {1, 1, 3}. Ana appears (twice in the list — irrelevant, membership is binary), Cleo appears, Ben does not. customers(id, name): Ana(1), Ben(2), Cleo(3). orders(customer_id) has rows: 1, NULL (one order's customer failed to record). I wrote SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) expecting Ben and Cleo. I got zero rows. Zero. Explain, and give me a version that works.

This is the most famous trap in SQL. NOT IN unfolds into a chain of inequalities: id <> 1 AND id <> NULL. For Ben (id 2): 2 <> 1 is true, but 2 <> NULL is UNKNOWN — NULL is not a value, so no comparison with it is ever true. True AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, and WHERE only passes TRUE. Every customer fails the same way, Cleo included, and Ana fails honestly on the first comparison. Result: nobody. One stray NULL in the subquery poisons the entire query.

The robust rewrite is NOT EXISTS, which tests existence rather than comparing values:

```sql
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);
```

Now the NULL order row simply never matches anyone, and you get Ben and Cleo. Rules to keep: NOT IN is safe only when the subquery column is guaranteed NOT NULL; when it might contain NULLs — or you are not sure — reach for NOT EXISTS. Defensively, NOT IN (SELECT ... WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL) also works, but NOT EXISTS says what you mean.

departments(id, name): Sales(1), Tech(2), Empty(3). employees(dept_id) has rows: 1, 1, 2. Explain what WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id) does when d is departments, why people write SELECT 1 instead of SELECT *, and how EXISTS differs from IN here.

EXISTS asks a yes/no question per department row: does at least one employee row exist with this department's id? Sales: yes (two employees). Tech: yes (one). Empty: no. Result: Sales and Tech.

It is a correlated subquery — the inner query references d.id from the outer row, so it is re-evaluated for each department. Semantically the engine may stop scanning at the first matching employee, because existence is all that matters; the second Sales employee adds nothing.

That is also why SELECT 1 is the convention: the subquery's select list is ignored entirely. EXISTS never looks at the values produced, only at whether a row was produced at all. SELECT 1, SELECT *, SELECT NULL all behave identically — the 1 is just a cheap placeholder that signals "existence check" to the reader.

Versus IN: for this positive membership question, IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees) returns the same Sales and Tech. The differences show up at the edges: IN materializes a list and compares values, so duplicates are harmless but NULLs in the list make NOT IN catastrophic (and leave IN itself fine for matched rows, though an unmatched outer row compared against a list containing NULL yields UNKNOWN, not FALSE — usually the same visible outcome, occasionally not). EXISTS never compares values at all, so NULLs cannot hurt it in either direction. When in doubt, EXISTS is the safer default for both directions.
